reference.source: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: Presents as an intensely itchy, chronic, relapsing dermatitis; itch is the cardinal symptom and often precedes visible changes
Distribution shifts with age: face and extensor surfaces in infants, flexural creases (antecubital and popliteal fossae) in older children and adults
Look for supporting features such as dry skin (xerosis), keratosis pilaris, and a personal or family history of atopy (asthma, allergic rhinitis)
The disease reflects impaired skin barrier plus immune dysregulation, so consistent emollient use is the foundation of every management plan
Flares are treated with topical corticosteroids of potency matched to site and severity, or with topical calcineurin inhibitors on delicate areas
Sudden worsening with weeping, crusting, or painful clustered vesicles suggests bacterial superinfection or eczema herpeticum, which needs prompt antiviral treatment
Identify and reduce trigger exposure (soaps, heat, sweat, aeroallergens, stress) and consider phototherapy or systemic immunomodulators for severe refractory disease
reference.pathophysiology: Atopic dermatitis arises from the interplay of a defective epidermal barrier and a skewed type-2 immune response. Loss-of-function variants in the filaggrin gene and reduced barrier lipids increase transepidermal water loss and allow penetration of allergens and microbes. This drives activation of type-2 cytokines (including interleukins 4, 13, and 31) that promote inflammation, further barrier breakdown, and the sensation of itch. Scratching perpetuates an itch-scratch cycle, causing lichenification, and the barrier defect predisposes to colonisation and infection with Staphylococcus aureus and herpes simplex virus.
additionalDifferentials: Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma in adult-onset recalcitrant disease
Immunodeficiency-associated dermatitis in infants with failure to thrive
additionalInvestigations: Primarily a clinical diagnosis based on morphology, distribution, and history
Bacterial swabs when infection or antibiotic resistance is suspected
Viral swab or PCR when eczema herpeticum is considered
Allergy testing (specific IgE or patch testing) only when a specific trigger is clinically suspected
Skin biopsy in atypical or treatment-resistant cases to exclude other diagnoses
redFlags: Eczema herpeticum: rapidly spreading painful monomorphic vesicles or punched-out erosions with systemic upset
Extensive secondary bacterial infection or signs of sepsis
Erythroderma with widespread inflammation and impaired thermoregulation
Failure to thrive or recurrent severe infection suggesting underlying immunodeficiency
reference.prognosis: Many children improve substantially or clear by adolescence, but a proportion have persistent or adult-onset disease; a relapsing course is typical and long-term control depends on barrier maintenance and trigger avoidance.
pitfalls: Under-treating flares with insufficiently potent topical steroids while over-worrying about steroid side effects
Neglecting regular generous emollient use, the cornerstone of maintenance
Missing eczema herpeticum and treating it as a routine bacterial flare
Attributing all disease to food allergy and pursuing unnecessary elimination diets
management: Establish liberal, regular emollient use as the foundation of every plan to restore the epidermal barrier, alongside avoidance of soaps, irritants and identified triggers
Treat flares with topical corticosteroids of potency matched to site and severity, using topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus or pimecrolimus) on the face, flexures and other delicate areas
Adopt proactive maintenance therapy to flare-prone sites and consider wet-wrap dressings and measures to break the itch-scratch cycle, including bedtime sedating antihistamines for sleep

Escalate moderate-to-severe disease to narrowband ultraviolet B phototherapy, systemic immunosuppression (ciclosporin, methotrexate or azathioprine) or targeted biologic and small-molecule therapy such as anti-interleukin-4/13 dupilumab or Janus kinase inhibitors
Treat bacterial superinfection with anti-staphylococcal antibiotics, and manage suspected eczema herpeticum urgently with systemic aciclovir
Refer to dermatology for refractory or diagnostically uncertain disease and arrange allergy assessment where a specific trigger is suspected
Educate patients and carers on emollient technique, corticosteroid safety and the relapsing course to support long-term adherence
